The hook's nightly-full-re-embed scenario is not a toy inefficiency but the default behavior of the naive version of this pipeline: without a hashing step, re-embedding cost scales with total corpus size every single night, forever, regardless of how little actually changed.

Reading a benchmark's own stated method (fixed sequence length, maximum batch size, a named hardware rate) before trusting its headline cost number is the general skill this topic teaches through one specific paper — the same discipline applies to any published throughput or latency claim, not only embedding benchmarks.

at.step: Reveal: throughput and cost per million tokens

items.item: An API rate limit and a GPU's compute ceiling are structurally different kinds of constraints: a rate limit is a fixed external cap unrelated to how much spare hardware exists, while a compute ceiling is a property of the hardware actually doing the work — conflating the two leads to optimizing throughput on hardware that was never the actual bottleneck.

Tombstone propagation and the label-leakage concern from topic 1 share the same shape even though they look unrelated: both are cases where data that should no longer be visible keeps being visible, and both are correctness failures rather than performance ones.

The incomparability of two models' vectors is not a limitation to work around with a translation layer; it is the reason a backfill needs a complete second index rather than any kind of incremental or partial conversion of the old vectors.

at.step: Reveal: why a model change cannot be an in-place swap

items.item: "Zero downtime" in a dual-index backfill specifically means no query is ever left with nothing to search, not that the backfill itself completes instantly — the backfill can take arbitrarily long as long as the old index keeps answering throughout it.

Qdrant's own soft-delete-plus-background-optimizer pattern and this topic's own dual-index backfill both separate "stop being visible immediately" from "finish the expensive physical work later" — the same two-phase shape recurs because an index's physical structure is expensive to touch and its logical correctness is not.

This topic's content-hash saving ratio depends entirely on how much of the corpus is actually unchanged on a given night; a corpus with a high edit rate would see a much smaller ratio, so the number this topic measures is a property of its own synthetic corpus, not a general constant.

The *(skipped)* embedding-model-choice topic is what would explain why two models' vectors land in different spaces in the first place; this topic deliberately states that fact and builds a procedure on top of it rather than re-deriving it, which is consistent with how CHAPTER.md scopes this topic's dependency on that skipped material.

The syllabus line's four clauses (throughput/cost, content hashing, tombstones, backfill) are four separate operational concerns that happen to all apply to the same kind of pipeline; a team could handle any one of them well while mishandling the others, so this topic teaches them as four distinct disciplines rather than one unified "embedding maintenance" procedure.
